title: Hunger, Thirst, and Satiety: How the Brain Controls Ingestion
kicker: Water Balance, Energy Regulation, Food Reward, and Eating Disorders
takeaways: Thirst uses both blood signals and advance information.
Osmotic and volume deficits recruit forebrain circuits; oral and gastrointestinal feedback can reduce drinking before absorbed water restores the blood.
Energy regulation coordinates several fuel stores.
Insulin, glucagon, liver glycogen, and adipose triglycerides distribute fuels across fed and fasting states; hunger is not a direct reading of one glucose value.
Hunger and satiation emerge from interacting populations.
AgRP, POMC, hypothalamic outputs, and brainstem populations change food seeking and consumption through specific transmitters and projections.
Gut signals carry more than fullness.
Distension, nutrient sensing, enteroendocrine secretion, and visceral afferents influence meal size and learned preference or avoidance through distinct routes.
Food reward and experience can alter intake.
Sensory cues, internal state, learned value, and social or environmental opportunities influence eating alongside immediate energy requirements.
Obesity and eating disorders require biological and behavioral care.
Genes, development, physiology, environment, and learning contribute; treatments engage different mechanisms and must be evaluated for the condition and person.
